scenes.title: The buried need
scenes.narration: A volunteer spends an hour mentoring a child. Before she leaves, she learns the family needs diapers tonight, so she posts a brief update. By morning it is buried under dozens of messages. The hour may never be counted. The family may still be waiting.
scenes.onScreenDisclosure: Illustrative reenactment · not a real chat provider

overlays.text: One update. One hour. Two people waiting.

scenes.title: Introduce the product
scenes.narration: This is the problem behind challenge five: coordinators rebuild their week from chats, texts and photos — forty volunteers, roughly four hours a week, reconstructed by hand. Volunteer Relay turns those updates into traceable records, and needs someone owns. Here is the coordinator's inbox, with review work waiting.

scenes.title: One everyday update
scenes.narration: Volunteers report in their own words. This update describes one shared garden visit, two volunteers, and the time each of them gave. Relay proposes an activity and two contributions, and keeps every proposed field tied to the original message. Nothing is approved until staff decide.
scenes.onScreenDisclosure: Authored demo proposal · no live model call

scenes.title: Inspect and approve
scenes.narration: One message holds a visit for two people. One shared hour means one visit and two volunteer-hours, so approving it records two separate contributions of sixty minutes each. Staff can inspect the evidence first, and anything missing or unresolved stays visible instead of being guessed. Nothing is guessed.

scenes.title: Duplicate report
scenes.narration: A later update describes the same visit. Counting every message would inflate the totals, so Relay raises the possible duplicate for staff review. Rejecting it leaves the approved ledger unchanged, and the decision stays attached to its source.

scenes.title: Ownership and acknowledgment
scenes.narration: An urgent need should never wait on a buried message. Staff assign an owner, set an acknowledgment deadline, and later record the outcome. If acknowledgment stalls, the worker escalates at the deadline. Delivery is not acknowledgment, and the board shows what still needs attention. An acknowledgment is a person taking responsibility, not a provider receipt.

overlays.text: An owner, not just an alert

scenes.title: Report with evidence
scenes.narration: At the end of the week the report comes from the same records the team used to do its work. Approved hours, contributions, open needs and pending items are counted consistently, and unknown time stays unknown rather than becoming zero. Every decision is kept in an audit history with its source, so the report and the work share one source of truth.

overlays.text: Approved time only · unknown stays unknown

scenes.title: Close
scenes.narration: Volunteer Relay. Every hour counted, every need connected. Built for nonprofit teams, with fictional demo data and an open-source implementation. The repository holds the code, the plan and the recording notes, including the fixtures used here.
